lesson.title: Adulthood and Aging: Development Doesn't Stop at Eighteen
lesson.summary: Physical, cognitive, and social development continue across adulthood: some abilities gradually decline, others stay stable or even improve, and social priorities shift in ways that often support emotional well-being in later life.
lesson.body:
It is tempting to think of development as something that happens to children and stops once a person reaches adulthood, but psychologists studying the lifespan find meaningful change continuing all the way through old age. Physical functioning generally peaks in young adulthood and then declines gradually. Sensory abilities such as vision and hearing often begin a slow decline starting in middle age, women typically go through menopause (the end of menstruation and fertility) in their late forties or early fifties, and male fertility declines gradually with age rather than ending at a sharp cutoff.

Cognitive aging is not a simple across-the-board decline. Psychologists distinguish between fluid intelligence, the ability to reason quickly and solve novel problems, and crystallized intelligence, the accumulated knowledge, vocabulary, and expertise a person has built up over a lifetime. Fluid intelligence tends to decline gradually starting in early or middle adulthood, but crystallized intelligence tends to remain stable and can even continue increasing into old age, which is one reason why vocabulary and general knowledge tests often show older adults performing as well as or better than younger adults even as processing speed slows.

Some decline in processing speed and in certain types of memory, particularly for new, unpracticed information, is a normal part of aging. This is an important distinction to hold onto: normal age-related memory change is not the same thing as a disease process like Alzheimer's disease, which involves a much more severe and progressive loss of memory and functioning and is not considered a typical part of aging.

Socially and emotionally, aging often brings changes that many people find surprisingly positive. One influential idea, socioemotional selectivity theory, proposes that as people come to perceive their remaining time as more limited, they shift their social priorities toward a smaller number of emotionally meaningful relationships rather than continuing to expand their social networks. This shift may help explain why measures of emotional well-being often hold steady, or even improve, in later adulthood despite the physical declines happening at the same time.

Taken together, adult and later-life development illustrates a theme that runs through this whole unit: change and continuity coexist. The adolescent brain changes described in the previous chapter do not stop developing at eighteen, and the physical and cognitive changes of aging show that development really is a lifelong process, not something confined to childhood.
